government.name: City of North Vancouver
government.howBuilt: This issue list draws on City of North Vancouver candidate websites and platforms, city news releases and news coverage of the 2026 campaign, including the North Shore wastewater plant costs and the 2025 parking plan. It keeps issues that city council can act on, such as zoning, the budget, parking, streets, city land and facilities. Provincial matters such as health care, and regional or provincial decisions such as bridge funding, are left out except where council has a direct role.

issues.title: Housing growth and density
issues.description: How quickly and in what form the city should add new homes through rezoning, pre-zoning and its community plan.
issues.whatItAffects: Housing supply and prices, neighbourhood scale, traffic and demand on schools, utilities and parks.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the Official Community Plan, zoning and rezoning decisions, within provincial housing-target and pre-zoning rules.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach new housing over the next four years?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add more homes of many types sooner, including through pre-zoning and faster approvals
viewQuestion.poleB: Pace new homes to area plans and infrastructure, with more case-by-case review

tradeoffs.context: Housing choices trade how fast new homes arrive against how much and how quickly neighbourhoods change.

gains: More homes could be built sooner, easing pressure on rents and prices
Clearer rules may shorten approval times for builders
costs: Roads, pipes and schools may lag behind new residents
Neighbourhoods may change faster than some residents want

gains: Growth may be easier to match with services and infrastructure
Residents may have more say on individual projects
costs: Fewer or slower new homes could keep prices higher
Longer reviews may add cost and uncertainty to projects

issues.title: Property taxes, spending and debt
issues.description: How much the city should raise property taxes and utility fees, borrow, and spend on capital projects, including rising regional sewage costs.
issues.whatItAffects: Property tax and utility bills for owners and renters, city debt levels and the services and projects the budget funds.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts the annual budget, five-year financial plan, tax rates, utility fees and borrowing; wastewater plant cost-sharing is set regionally by Metro Vancouver.

viewQuestion.question: What should guide the city's budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Hold down tax and utility increases by limiting new spending and borrowing
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep investing in services and infrastructure even if taxes rise more

tradeoffs.context: Budget choices trade lower bills now against the level of services and the condition of city assets later.

gains: Smaller increases in tax and utility bills for households and businesses
Less debt may leave more room for future emergencies
costs: Some services, maintenance or projects may be delayed or reduced
Deferred upkeep can cost more when it is finally done

gains: Services, facilities and infrastructure may be maintained or expanded
Projects can proceed before costs rise further
costs: Higher tax and utility bills for owners, and often renters
More borrowing adds interest costs to future budgets

issues.title: Street space and getting around
issues.description: How the city divides street space among driving, transit, walking, cycling and micromobility, and what it advocates for on rapid transit and bridges.
issues.whatItAffects: Commute times, congestion, road safety, bus reliability and the feel of main streets like Lonsdale.
issues.whoDecides: Council controls city streets, its mobility plan, traffic calming and bike lanes; TransLink and the province fund rapid transit and highway crossings.

viewQuestion.question: How should city streets be used?
viewQuestion.poleA: Give more street space to transit, walking and cycling, even if driving lanes are reduced
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep main roads flowing for vehicles and limit reductions in driving lanes

tradeoffs.context: Street space is fixed, so adding room for one way of travel usually means less for another.

gains: Faster, more reliable buses and safer walking and cycling routes
May reduce car trips over time as other options improve
costs: Drivers may face slower trips or fewer lanes
Projects can disrupt businesses and residents during construction

gains: Vehicle traffic and deliveries may move more smoothly on arterials
Fewer changes to roads residents already rely on
costs: Transit, walking and cycling improvements may come more slowly
Congestion may persist as the population grows

issues.title: Pay parking and curb access
issues.description: Whether to keep, adjust or roll back the city's expanded pay parking introduced under its 2025 Curb Access and Parking Plan.
issues.whatItAffects: Cost and availability of street parking for residents, visitors and customers of local businesses, and city parking revenue.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets parking zones, rates, hours and permit rules by bylaw.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city do with its pay parking system?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep pay parking largely as is to manage curb demand and turnover
viewQuestion.poleB: Scale back pay parking hours or areas and revise the plan

tradeoffs.context: Parking policy trades easy, low-cost parking against turnover, curb space for other uses and city revenue.

gains: More open spaces through turnover for shoppers and deliveries
Parking revenue helps fund city services
costs: Visitors, workers and some businesses pay more to park
Some drivers may avoid paid areas or park in nearby streets

gains: Lower parking costs for residents, visitors and customers
Evening and weekend visits may be easier for some businesses
costs: Spaces may fill up more, making parking harder to find
Lost revenue may need to be made up elsewhere in the budget

issues.title: Protections for renters
issues.description: How strongly the city should protect tenants displaced when older rental buildings are redeveloped.
issues.whatItAffects: Compensation, relocation help and return rights for renters, and the cost of redeveloping older rental buildings.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the tenant displacement policy and rental-replacement conditions through rezoning and bylaws, alongside provincial tenancy law.

viewQuestion.question: How far should city tenant protections go?
viewQuestion.poleA: Require stronger compensation and right-to-return terms for displaced renters
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep requirements moderate so rental redevelopment stays viable

tradeoffs.context: Tenant rules trade security for current renters against the pace and cost of replacing older buildings.

gains: Displaced renters may be able to stay in the community
Long-term tenants get more certainty during redevelopment
costs: Higher costs may delay or cancel some rental projects
Costs may be passed on in rents for new units

gains: More rental redevelopment may proceed, adding new units
Simpler rules may speed up approvals
costs: Displaced renters may have to leave the city
Less certainty for long-term tenants in older buildings

issues.title: Use of city-owned land
issues.description: Whether city-owned sites, such as the 100 block of East 1st Street, should be used for housing or development, or kept as public space or park.
issues.whatItAffects: Supply of parks and open space, potential housing or revenue from city land, and how dense areas like Lower Lonsdale feel.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides the zoning, sale, lease or park designation of land the city owns.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city use land it owns?
viewQuestion.poleA: Use suitable city land for housing or development, including below-market homes
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep key city land public, as park or open space, rather than develop or sell it

tradeoffs.context: City land is limited, so each site used for one purpose is unavailable for another.

gains: New homes or below-market units on land the city controls
Sales or leases can bring revenue for other city priorities
costs: Less green and open space in growing neighbourhoods
Land sold may not be available for future public needs

gains: More parks and open space for a denser population
The city keeps long-term control of the land
costs: Fewer opportunities to add housing the city can steer
Lost revenue and ongoing park costs

issues.title: Public input and how decisions are made
issues.description: How much consultation, public input time and reporting the city should provide before and after major decisions.
issues.whatItAffects: How residents are heard on projects and budgets, and how long approvals and decisions take.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets its procedure bylaw, engagement processes and reporting practices.

viewQuestion.question: How should council balance consultation and speed?
viewQuestion.poleA: Expand consultation and public input before major decisions, even if it takes longer
viewQuestion.poleB: Streamline processes so decisions and approvals move faster

tradeoffs.context: More input can improve decisions and trust but adds time and cost.

gains: Residents may have more influence on decisions that affect them
Concerns may surface before projects are approved
costs: Decisions and approvals may take longer
More engagement processes add staff costs

gains: Projects and permits may move ahead faster
Lower process costs for the city and applicants
costs: Some residents may feel less heard
Problems may be found later, after decisions are made

issues.title: Child care, recreation and community facilities
issues.description: How much the city should invest in child care spaces, recreation centres, fields and other community facilities as it grows.
issues.whatItAffects: Access to child care and recreation, facility upkeep costs and the city's capital budget.
issues.whoDecides: Council funds and builds city facilities, secures amenities from developers and partners with senior governments on child care.

viewQuestion.question: How much should the city invest in community facilities?
viewQuestion.poleA: Expand child care, recreation and community facilities to keep up with growth
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on maintaining existing facilities and limit new capital spending

tradeoffs.context: New facilities serve a growing population but bring building, staffing and upkeep costs.

gains: More child care spaces and recreation options
Facilities keep pace as more residents arrive
costs: Higher capital and operating costs, often paid through taxes
More borrowing may be needed

gains: Lower capital spending and less new debt
Existing facilities may be better maintained
costs: Waitlists for child care and programs may grow
Facilities may become crowded as the city grows

issues.title: Trees, climate and resilience
issues.description: How strongly the city should protect trees, expand its canopy and require climate measures in buildings and infrastructure.
issues.whatItAffects: Urban tree cover, summer heat, stormwater, emissions and development costs.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets tree bylaws, development requirements, climate targets and infrastructure spending.

viewQuestion.question: How strongly should the city prioritize trees and climate measures?
viewQuestion.poleA: Strengthen tree protection and climate requirements, even if projects cost more
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep requirements flexible to limit costs and delays for homes and projects

tradeoffs.context: Climate and tree rules bring long-term benefits but can add upfront cost and complexity.

gains: More shade and cooler streets during heat waves
Better handling of stormwater and lower emissions
costs: Higher costs and longer timelines for some projects
Fewer homes may fit on some sites

gains: Lower costs and simpler approvals for builders
More flexibility in site design
costs: Tree canopy may shrink as sites redevelop
Higher long-term climate and heat risks

election.howToVote: Eligible City of North Vancouver electors can vote on General Voting Day, Saturday, Oct. 17 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m.), at voting places including schools, Harry Jerome Community Recreation Centre, John Braithwaite Community Centre and The Pipe Shop, or at advance voting at City Hall on Oct. 7, 10, 13, 14 and 15. Voters who are not already registered can register at the voting place by showing two pieces of ID that together prove identity and residential address, at least one with a signature; non-resident property electors also need proof of property ownership. Check cnv.org/vote for the full list of voting places and accepted ID.
election.voteByMail: Mail ballot voting was available to electors who applied by Oct. 1, 2026; the city's election page has instructions for returning mail ballots.

candidates.name: Linda Buchanan
candidates.summary: Mayor since 2018 and a city councillor from 2011 to 2018; previously a North Vancouver school trustee. Worked about 30 years as a public health nurse and was born and raised in North Vancouver.

positions.summary: Supports delivering hundreds of new homes of many types, including ground-oriented and missing-middle housing and below-market rentals.
positions.leanReason: Favours adding more homes of several types

positions.summary: Commits to strengthening the city's residential tenant displacement policy and updating its mid-market rental policy.
Champions Burrard Inlet Rapid Transit and regional transit links for the North Shore.
Highlights new child care spaces and delivering the Harry Jerome Community Recreation Centre.
positions.leanReason: Supports expanding city facilities and services

positions.summary: Highlights a 2026 financial plan with a 0.9% operating tax increase plus 2% for capital, and longer-term asset and reserve planning.
positions.leanReason: Cites both restraint and capital investment

candidates.name: Dave Kurvers
candidates.summary: Has worked more than three decades in B.C.'s film and television industry and served on Elections BC's Election Advisory Committee.

positions.summary: Would seek a provincial exemption from pre-zoning rules and require a city-planned alternative when developers seek major plan amendments.
Would reverse residential zoning of city-owned East First Street lands and designate them a park; opposes selling public land.
positions.leanReason: Keep city land public as park

positions.summary: Proposes a right for long-term renters displaced by redevelopment to return at comparable rents, with moving and interim housing help.
Opposes elevated SkyTrain on the North Shore; supports cycling routes where they make sense and curb space for loading and accessible parking.
positions.leanReason: Mixed; does not clearly favour either pole

positions.summary: Proposes set permit turnaround times, capital project dashboards for projects over $10 million, and budget stress tests.
positions.leanReason: Both faster permits and more reporting

positions.summary: Would keep annual tax increases close to inflation where practical and direct growth revenue first to reserves, infrastructure or debt reduction.
positions.leanReason: Limit tax increases and new spending

positions.summary: Wants curb space kept for short-term access and deliveries, opposes app-only parking payment and supports permits for resident work vehicles.
positions.leanReason: Adjusts parking design; no clear stance on scaling back

candidates.name: Mike McGraw
candidates.summary: Founder of a local software company and a former school trustee; has served on the library board and is a strata council president. Has lived in North Vancouver for decades.

positions.summary: Says infrastructure must be planned before density, and wants a full Capilano Mall and Marine Drive plan before individual rezonings.
positions.leanReason: Growth tied to plans and infrastructure first

positions.summary: Wants the 100 block of East 1st Street as parkland and all options examined before selling significant public land.
Proposes a long-term capital and debt plan and pressing Metro Vancouver for fairer sharing of wastewater plant costs.
Would hold consultation before major decisions, expand verbal public input at council, and publish a major-project accountability dashboard.
Supports a meaningful right to return for tenants and a city-run renter concierge service.
Calls for walking, cycling and transit capacity alongside the roads residents rely on, with projects modelled together and results measured.

candidates.name: Holly Back
candidates.summary: City councillor since 2014 and former North Vancouver school trustee; ran a salon and school on Lonsdale for 20 years and taught at Carson Graham. Born and raised in North Vancouver.

positions.summary: Supports pre-zoning for smaller lots, workforce housing, below-market units, coach houses and rent-to-own options.
Supports increasing public input time at council from two to three minutes.
Names Ironworkers Memorial Bridge congestion a top priority and would press senior governments for lanes, transit or a new bridge.
Supports more emergency shelter space and warming centres.

candidates.name: Don Bell
candidates.summary: City councillor and former MP for North Vancouver, District of North Vancouver mayor and school board chair; a North Vancouver resident for over 57 years who owned a small retail business.

positions.summary: Prioritizes reducing tax increases for residents and businesses and supports an independent inquiry into wastewater plant costs.
Says pay parking created unintended consequences that can be mitigated with some adjustments.
Would improve protection of mature trees and expand the city's tree canopy.
Supports expanding recreation and sports facilities, courts, parks and child care access for a growing population.
Wants more effective direct public engagement and transparency with better ways to connect with council.

candidates.name: Tammy Bentz
candidates.summary: BCIT instructor and stage and screen actor, writer and director; a former national councillor of the Canadian Actors' Equity Association who ran federally for the NDP in North Vancouver in 2021.

candidates.name: Anna Boltenko
candidates.summary: Leadership coach and founder of the North Shore Kids Festival; has served over eight years on city advisory committees, including chairing the Social Planning Advisory Committee, and sits on the Advisory Planning Commission.

positions.summary: Says new residential development must be matched by roads, transit, childcare, schools, recreation and utilities.
Wants City Hall to communicate openly about budgets, procurement and neighbourhood impacts, with early public engagement.
Supports street and public space improvements for people walking, cycling, using transit, pushing strollers or with disabilities.
Supports safe play spaces, childcare access, recreation programs and children's mental health prevention.

candidates.name: Jeremy Cato
candidates.summary: Creator of a YouTube channel on North Shore civic issues; says he has spent four years studying the city's finances and plans.

positions.summary: Opposes net road capacity reductions on bridge-feeding corridors until funded transit alternatives exist.
Would link major rezonings to named transportation infrastructure requests and coordinate traffic and growth decisions.
Proposes a debt dashboard and a reserve-floor policy, citing a historic debt-servicing load.
Proposes the old ICBC site as a mix of community hub, cultural centre, housing and business centre.
positions.leanReason: Develop city-linked site for mixed uses

candidates.name: Angela Girard
candidates.summary: City of North Vancouver councillor since 2018, seeking a third term.

positions.summary: Cites strengthening tenant protections during redevelopment and the city's high rate of rental housing construction.
Highlights expanding child care, including on city land, and delivering Harry Jerome and Silver Harbour centres.
Advocated a cooling strategy limiting indoor temperatures to 26 C in multi-unit buildings.
Cites a 2026 HUB Cycling award for the city's active transportation work.

candidates.name: Guy Heywood
candidates.summary: Former two-term City of North Vancouver councillor and three-term school trustee; a CPA who has advised companies and First Nations on financing. Has lived in North Vancouver for decades.

positions.summary: Says the city's finances and rising utility and property tax bills are hurting affordability for homeowners and renters.
positions.leanReason: Focus on reducing tax and fee pressure

positions.summary: Argues the Harry Jerome recreation centre decision badly strained city finances.
Criticizes current public consultation as costly and says the city does not listen to what residents want.
positions.leanReason: Wants responsiveness but critical of consultation processes

candidates.name: Ken Izatt
candidates.summary: North Vancouver resident for more than 45 years, recently retired from a business career; served six years on the city's Social Planning Advisory Committee and as treasurer of the MONOVA friends society.

positions.summary: Would end paid parking at 6 p.m., review the whole parking system and add accessible spaces.
Would prioritize infrastructure, safety and maintenance over discretionary spending and challenge regional wastewater cost-sharing.
positions.leanReason: Limit spending to hold down increases

positions.summary: Would review the 2022 Mobility Plan and keep main arterials like Lonsdale and Keith Road flowing rather than reduce road space.
Proposes a binding bylaw guaranteeing compensation and right of first refusal for displaced tenants.
Would convert the vacant 100 block of East 1st Street into a permanent public park.

candidates.name: Jullian Kolstee
candidates.summary: Improv theatre coach, performer and culture strategist for a medical device manufacturer; grew up in North Vancouver and attended Capilano University.

positions.summary: Supports mixed-use density along transit corridors, small-scale multi-unit homes in residential areas and more non-market housing.
Supports stronger tenant protections alongside expanded non-market housing.
Would advocate for bus rapid transit expansion and build out active transportation networks.
positions.leanReason: More space for transit and active modes

positions.summary: Would pursue a public inquiry into the wastewater treatment plant and monitor city debt and reserves.
positions.leanReason: Oversight, no clear side on tax levels

positions.summary: Proposes increasing tree canopy, improving drainage and reviewing emergency plans to reduce climate risks.

candidates.name: Max Lai
candidates.summary: Education assistant born on the North Shore; studied political science at Simon Fraser University. Running for council for the first time.

positions.summary: Would expand the Housing Initiatives Grant and simplify zoning so homeowners can convert single-family lots into multiplexes.
Proposes that new rental developments secure at least 30% of units as affordable and 20% for workers earning $30,000-$80,000.
positions.leanReason: Affordability requirement; not on an issue scale

positions.summary: Supports updating the mobility strategy with a detailed transit plan and more than one bus rapid transit line on the North Shore.
Supports a $25 low-income transit pass and a city-operated, not-for-profit grocery store.
positions.leanReason: Not tied to an issue scale

candidates.name: Jessica McIlroy
candidates.summary: City councillor since 2018 and North Vancouver resident since 2006; has worked over 20 years in sustainability leadership roles, including as a non-profit executive director.

positions.summary: Chairs the city's Climate and Environment Task Force and has championed updated emissions targets and climate resilience funding.
Supports more mobility options and has pursued intersection safety measures and speed limit pilots.
positions.leanReason: More travel options and safety measures

positions.summary: Lists expanding a diversity of housing options for all residents as a goal.

candidates.name: Krishna Raisinghani
candidates.summary: Chair of the city's Advisory Planning Commission with nearly two decades in strategy, finance and planning roles; grew up on the North Shore.

positions.summary: Supports diverse housing types and streamlined approvals, with infrastructure developed alongside growth and targets for essential worker housing.
Would strengthen renter protections with relocation support and return pathways for displaced tenants.
Would reassess pay parking rates and policies and publish yearly reports on outcomes.
Proposes earlier engagement, quarterly scorecards on progress and costs, and quarterly community office hours.

candidates.name: Andrew Robertson
candidates.summary: Medical physicist and clinical investigator at BC Cancer and UBC clinical instructor; grew up in North Vancouver and is president of the BC Association of Medical Physicists.

positions.summary: Supports townhomes, rowhouses and multiplexes, fewer barriers to multigenerational homes, and lower permitting delays for new homes.
Would expand non-market housing through dedicating city land and explore community land trusts.
Supports more transit, North Shore rapid transit, better bus stops and complete cycling networks.
positions.leanReason: More space for transit and active modes

positions.summary: Would grow the tree canopy, retain trees in developments and use green stormwater infrastructure.
Supports protecting renters displaced by development.

candidates.name: Shervin Shahriari
candidates.summary: City councillor since 2022; business and project management lecturer at Langara and former senior planning manager at TransLink. Moved to North Vancouver in 1984 and chaired the city library board.

positions.summary: Opposed expanding pay parking to seven days a week, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Calls for thorough community engagement before any major decision.
Prioritizes retaining mature healthy trees and heritage buildings in development.
Calls for stronger financial analysis before approving new projects and raised concerns about wastewater plant costs.
Would require new developments to provide adequate off-street parking.

candidates.name: Lailani Tumaneng
candidates.summary: Registered nurse with 26 years at Vancouver Coastal Health and a North Vancouver school trustee elected in 2022; has lived in North Vancouver for more than 30 years.

positions.summary: Names community safety, climate change and sustainability, affordable housing and equitable governance as her main focus areas.
positions.leanReason: General priorities; no side on an issue scale

candidates.name: Tony Valente
candidates.summary: City councillor seeking re-election; senior director of infrastructure and capital projects at a B.C. Crown corporation, former chair of HUB Cycling's North Shore committee and holds a UBC MBA.

positions.summary: Supports protected mobility lanes, e-bike safety and more bus and walking options to give residents choices beyond driving.
positions.leanReason: More street space for non-car modes

positions.summary: Supports more housing options, including condos, apartments and duplexes.
Supports strengthening renter protections during redevelopment.
Supports bus rapid transit with dedicated lanes and a new Second Narrows crossing that enables transit.
Supports more parklets, pocket parks, dog parks, street trees and courts as neighbourhoods densify.

notes: City of North Vancouver (not the District). 4 mayoral and 18 council candidates for 6 seats; the candidate list matches the city's 2026 announcement and an independent listing (northvanvotes.ca), used only to confirm names and websites, since cnv.org pages load content by script and the fetch tool could not read the official candidate list, profiles or voting details. Advance voting dates, hours and voting places come from candidate websites (shahriari.ca/get-involved, corroborated by donbell.ca) restating city information; verify at cnv.org/vote. No elector organizations or ballot questions were found for the city. The six incumbent councillors (Back, Bell, Girard, McIlroy, Shahriari, Valente) and Mayor Buchanan are running again; incumbency is confirmed by 2022 results (Global News). Guy Heywood is a former two-term councillor. North Shore News Q&A with all candidates returned 403 and could not be used. No position statements found for Oliver King (website kingofparliament.ca would not resolve), Sean Alexander (site loads content by script; not read), David Brun (no website or coverage found) or Tammy Bentz (tammybentz.ca still shows her 2021 federal NDP page; bio is from it). Lailani Tumaneng has no website; her bio and priorities come from a Reyfort Media profile. Some positions from the earlier run (Boltenko, Buchanan, Kurvers, McGraw) were kept as written; Buchanan, Kurvers and McGraw pages were re-checked. Tony Valente's first-election year was not stated consistently on his site and is omitted. csdId 5915051 not re-verified against StatCan this run. Leans are proposals for review.
